content: 1. It is crucial for pharmacists, pharmacy workers, and community health workers to be adequately trained to identify the signs and symptoms of complications following an abortion. 2. Post-abortion contraception can be initiated immediately after a surgical or medical abortion (first or second trimester, including after a septic abortion) using combined hormonal contraceptives (CHCs), progestin-only contraceptives (POCs), or barrier methods such as condoms, spermicides, diaphragms, and caps. However, diaphragms and caps are unsuitable until six weeks after a second-trimester abortion. 3. Intrauterine devices (IUDs) can be inserted immediately after a first-trimester surgical or medical abortion without restrictions (MEC Category 1). For second-trimester abortions, IUDs can be inserted with caution (MEC Category 2, where benefits outweigh risks). However, IUDs should not be inserted immediately after a septic abortion due to the risk of exacerbating the condition (MEC Category 4). 4. Fertility-awareness-based (FAB) methods, particularly symptom-based methods, should be used with caution after an abortion, as they may require special counseling to ensure proper use. Calendar-based methods should be delayed until the individual’s condition is fully evaluated, and temporary alternative contraceptive methods should be offered in the meantime. 5. For individuals undergoing surgical abortion and wishing to use contraception, it is recommended to offer the option of initiating contraception at the time of the surgical procedure. However, the quality of evidence supporting this recommendation is very low. 6. For individuals undergoing medical abortion with mifepristone and misoprostol or misoprostol alone: Hormonal contraception (e.g., pills, patches, rings, implants, or injections) can be initiated immediately after the first pill of the medical abortion regimen. IUD placement should be performed only after confirming the success of the abortion procedure. 7. Immediate initiation of intramuscular depot medroxyprogesterone acetate (DMPA) after a medical abortion is associated with a slight reduction in the effectiveness of the abortion regimen. However, it remains a viable contraceptive option and should still be offered. 8. There is no available data on the use of combined hormonal contraceptives (pills or injections) during medical abortion. Individuals opting for contraceptive rings should be advised to check for expulsion during heavy bleeding associated with the abortion process. 9. Insertion and removal of IUDs should be performed by trained professionals, including auxiliary nurse midwives, nurses, midwives, associate/advanced associate clinicians, generalist medical practitioners, and specialist medical practitioners. In some contexts, traditional and complementary medicine professionals (TCMPs) and auxiliary nurses may also perform these tasks under specific conditions, such as established health system mechanisms or rigorous research settings. 10. Contraceptive implants should be inserted or removed by nurses, midwives, associate/advanced associate clinicians, generalist medical practitioners, and specialist medical practitioners. Community health workers (CHWs), TCMPs, and auxiliary nurses may also perform these tasks under specific conditions, such as rigorous research or targeted monitoring and evaluation. 11. Injectable contraceptives can be administered by individuals themselves, community health workers, pharmacy workers, pharmacists, TCMPs, auxiliary nurses, nurses, midwives, associate/advanced associate clinicians, generalist medical practitioners, and specialist medical practitioners. Self-administration involves the use of syringes, either intramuscularly or subcutaneously, and compact pre-filled auto-disable devices have been developed to facilitate this process. 12. Over-the-counter oral contraceptive pills (OCPs) should be made available without a prescription to individuals who wish to use them. 13. Emergency contraceptive pills should also be made available over the counter without a prescription for individuals seeking emergency contraception. 14. The consistent and correct use of male and female condoms is highly effective in preventing the sexual transmission of HIV, reducing the risk of HIV transmission in serodiscordant couples, lowering the risk of acquiring other sexually transmitted infections (STIs) and associated conditions (e.g., genital warts and cervical cancer), and preventing unintended pregnancies. 15. Telemedicine should be offered as an alternative to in-person interactions for delivering medical abortion services. This includes eligibility assessment, counseling, instructions for administering medications, and follow-up care, all conducted remotely. 16. Self-management of medical abortion (for pregnancies under 12 weeks) should be an available option. This includes self-assessment of eligibility, self-administration of abortion medications outside a healthcare facility, and self-assessment of the success of the abortion. However, individuals must have access to accurate information, quality-assured medications (including pain management), trained health worker support, and healthcare facilities or referral services if needed. 17. Restrictions on prescribing and dispensing abortion medications may need to be modified to facilitate self-management within the regulatory framework of the health system.
